newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal defends its World War Two gold trade.
newsitem.headline: Portugal defends its World War Two gold trade.

text.p: Portugal's central bank on Wednesday said that a huge build-up in its gold reserves during World War Two reflected legitimate trade and there was no suggestion of "laundering" of illicit Nazi funds.
Presenting a first report into its gold dealings during the war years, the Bank said that nearly half of the bullion had in any case been bought from the Federal Reserve, the U.S. central bank.

"From an initial analysis, there is no evidence of any laundering activity," said economic historian Joaquim Costa Leite who has been brought in by the Bank to carry out a probe into its gold transactions in the years 1937-1946.

Portugal was, after Switzerland, the second largest recipient of gold from Nazi Germany, stoking suspicion that much of the bullion had been looted from occupied countries or even from Jews murdered in concentration camps.

In an effort to quieten concerns, particularly from international Jewish groups, the Bank and the government have opened state archives to allow for an investigation into all gold deals during those years when the country was ruled by a rightwing dictatorship.
The first report drawn up by Costa Leite showed that gold reserves held by the Bank leapt from 67 tonnes in 1937 to some 370 tonnes in 1946.
Some 48 percent of this bullion was bought from the United States, with 30 percent coming from Switzerland and 14 percent from the Reichsbank, the then German central bank.
Portugal has long held that gold was received from Germany to settle debts from trade, which as an officially neutral country, it was allowed to carry out with the Axis countries.
Added to that was the fact that throughout the early 1930s Portugal had already begun increasing its stock of gold because it saw it as the only secure international asset.
Wartime purchases were just an extention of this policy, Costa Leite said.

The preliminary report only set out to clarify from whom Portugal had been buying gold during the period and work had still not started on the 4ensitive question of whether any it was looted, the investigator told a news conference, flanked by senior Bank officials.
A senior Jewish official said recently that it was highly likely that some of the gold bought by Portugal had been stolen from Holocaust victims.

Maram Stern, assistant secretary-general of the World Jewish Congress, said in Lisbon, where he had come for talks with Bank officials, that the Nazis had stolen so much gold from concentration camp victims that it was "logical" that some of it had turned up here.

Under an agreement reached with the Allied Powers at the end of the war, Portugal returned some four tonnes of gold which was suspected of having been stolen from the Belgian and Dutch central banks by Nazi troops at the start of the war.
